paper_title: TRIC: A Thermal Resistance and Impedance Calculator for Electronic Packages

extraction.paper_title: TRIC: A Thermal Resistance and Impedance Calculator for Electronic Packages

scenario.description: Thermal impedance ZTHJA vs. time of a 10 × 10 mm² eTQFP with a 6 × 6 mm² epad for four different die sizes (2×2, 3×3, 4×4, 5×5 mm²), dissipating 1 W via a power step applied at t=0
scenario.architecture: 10×10 mm² eTQFP package; 6×6 mm² exposed pad; rectangular parallelepiped mesh; Manhattan geometry; epad lead frame with depressed die pad; leads extending from all four sides; single heat source on die
scenario.workload: Power step: 1 W applied instantaneously at t=0 to single heat source; uniform power distribution over die surface; junction-to-ambient (ϑJA) thermal path; static conditions reached at approximately 400 s
scenario.operating_point: Transient thermal response from t=10⁻⁵ s to t=10³ s; ambient temperature Tamb=20°C (inferred from Section 4.3); junction temperature rise over ambient normalized to 1 W input power; no active cooling beyond natural convection

original_setup.solver: Finite Volume (FV) method based; TRIC uses model-order reduction (MOR) with multigrid iterative solver for complex frequency domain equations
original_setup.optimizer: Projection-based approach (Algorithms 1-3); parametric model-order reduction without traditional optimization
original_setup.controller: None; passive thermal system with boundary conditions defined per JEDEC ambient specifications
original_setup.benchmark: FloTHERM v12.2 (Mentor Graphics) for validation; JEDEC thermal metrics (ϑJA, ΨJB, ΨJCtop, ϑJB, ϑJCtop, ϑJCbottom)

thermal_observable.aggregation: point measurement at die center or heat source center; thermal impedance ZTHJA = ϑJA(t) defined as temperature rise normalized to applied power

physical_mismatches.reason: TRIC is a compact thermal model extraction tool, not a direct thermal simulation of actual packaged devices; relies on simplified Manhattan geometry pDTMs with aggregate properties (e.g., weighted-average lead thermal conductivity) rather than explicit die, lead, and mold geometry

Boundary conditions are idealized per JEDEC standards (e.g., extremely high heat transfer coefficient on bottom surface for ϑJCbottom) rather than realistic thermal interface materials or mounting conditions
No transient heat generation profile data provided for the eTQFP scenario; Figure 6 uses artificial power step input (1 W step at t=0) not representative of actual semiconductor operation
Multi-source analysis (Section 4.4) considers only static layouts with fixed heat source positions; does not model dynamic power distribution or thermal coupling feedback during transient operation

studio_assumptions: Purely conductive heat transfer (no convection or radiation explicitly modeled within package); convection implicit in boundary conditions
Board modeled as single finely-meshed parallelepiped with adjusted thermal conductivity to represent aggregate metal traces and vias
Pins and leads represented as single rectangular parallelepiped with weighted-average thermal conductivity (not detailed geometry)
Die attach material properties assumed constant; glue type selectable but properties not explicitly documented
Steady-state and transient solutions derived from linear thermal resistance/capacitance network via projection onto reduced basis
Intrinsic package symmetry exploited: only quarter-structure meshed with adiabatic boundary conditions on symmetry planes
Non-Manhattan variations (e.g., pLQFP die position shift with thickness change, multi-source die layouts) handled via geometric coordinate transformation and projection basis adaptation
Mesh convergence: discretization chosen to achieve ≤0.1% inaccuracy based on prior convergence study (reference [11])

methods.note: TRIC uses model-order reduction (MOR) via projection-based Algorithms 1–3 with multigrid iterative solver in complex frequency domain. Parametric detailed thermal models (pDTMs) with rectangular parallelepiped mesh (Manhattan geometry) and non-Manhattan transformations are handled. Convergence criterion of 0.1% inaccuracy is documented in Section 2. Methods match abstract claim of 'novel projection-based approach.'

code.note: No source code repository, executable binary, or supplementary material link provided. Figure 2 shows example DTM meshes but no mesh files, CAD models, or code accessible. Graphical user interface mentioned but not publicly available. Reproducibility requires access to TRIC software not supplied in paper or assets.

parameters.note: Package parameters clearly enumerated in Section 2: eTQFP body sizes 10×10 mm², epad sizes 6×6 mm², die sizes 2×2 to 5×5 mm² for Figure 6. eTQFP body thickness 1 mm (eTQFP variant). Power step 1 W applied at t=0 stated in caption. Ambient temperature 20°C confirmed in Section 4.3. Figure 6 shows four die sizes with legend labels 2×2, 3×3, 4×4, 5×5 mm².

config.note: JEDEC thermal metrics configuration (ϑJA, ΨJB, ΨJCtop, ϑJB, ϑJCtop, ϑJCbottom) for four standard ambients per Section 2. Boundary conditions idealized per JEDEC standards. Board modeled as single finely-meshed parallelepiped with aggregate thermal conductivity. Leads represented as weighted-average parallelepiped. Symmetry exploitation: quarter-structure meshed with adiabatic BCs on symmetry planes (Section 4). Configuration consistent across all reported scenarios.

findings.reason: Section 2 references prior convergence study from [11] (TRAC paper) establishing 0.1% discretization inaccuracy criterion. Figure 6 scenario may use different geometry or finer mesh than [11] convergence study, but applicability to this specific case not verified in present paper.

findings.reason: JEDEC metric ϑJA is 'junction-to-ambient thermal resistance' but paper does not define which die location represents the junction (die center, maximum temperature point, area-weighted average, or specified probing location). Figure 2 shows 'temperature probes' (black circles) but their exact coordinates relative to die boundaries not specified.

findings.reason: Section 2 states board modeled as 'single finely-meshed parallelepiped with thermal conductivity adjusted to account for aggregate effect of metal traces and vias.' This lumped representation may not capture actual PCB layer stack or via thermal vias, limiting model fidelity for applications where board thermal path is critical.

findings.reason: Section 2 states 'Various types of glue for die attach can be selected' but no table of glue types with thermal conductivity or thickness values provided. Die attach material strongly influences transient thermal response at short times (<1 ms).
findings.locator: Section 2 (page 3): 'Various types of glue for die attach can be selected' without property details.

findings.reason: Figure 6 shows time axis from 10⁻⁵ to 10³ seconds (logarithmic scale). At t=10⁻⁵ s, thermal impedance ~25 K/W for 2×2 mm² die. At t=1 s, curves show rapid decay. Physical interpretation of initial transient (t<1 ms) is unclear: this may reflect numerical initialization artifacts rather than real die thermal inertia if mesh timestep is not sufficiently fine.

assessment.summary: Paper W3021197939 (TRIC: A Thermal Resistance and Impedance Calculator for Electronic Packages) describes a compact thermal model extraction tool for eTQFP, eLQFP, pLQFP, eQFN, and related packages. Figure 6 on page 7 presents transient thermal impedance ZTHJA versus time for a 10×10 mm² eTQFP with 6×6 mm² epad under 1 W power step, parameterized across die sizes (2×2 to 5×5 mm²). The scenario is fundamentally illustrative of the TRIC methodology rather than a reproducible experimental validation dataset. The paper validates TRIC against FloTHERM v12.2 with reported <3% discrepancy and 15–20× CPU speedup, but does not provide sufficient implementation detail (mesh dimensions, material properties, full boundary condition specifications, or code/data repositories) to enable independent replication. Studio cannot execute this scenario because: (1) the experiment type is declared as custom_2d_steady but lacks floorplan blocks and power_w mapping required for instantiation; (2) the scenario describes a 3D transient thermal simulation (transient time-domain response from 10⁻⁵ s to 10³ s), contradicting the steady-state label; (3) essential input parameters such as die thickness, detailed material properties, and mesh discretization are missing or stated only in context of other package families; (4) no digital artifact (source code, CAD, or supplementary data) is linked or available for cross-validation. The scenario is classified as not_2d_applicable because thermal packaging analysis in TRIC inherently requires 3D representation of die, epad, mold, leads, and board geometry with full spatial detail; 2D approximations are explicitly not supported by the tool's architecture.
limitations: Experiment metadata declares custom_2d_steady type but provides neither floorplan blocks nor power_w object; Studio input validation gate fails immediately.
Scenario describes transient 3D thermal impedance evolution (time-dependent heat diffusion from 10⁻⁵ s to 10³ s), incompatible with steady-state 2D assumption; temporal regime mismatch.

Die thickness for Figure 6 not explicitly stated; paper mentions 100, 280, 375, 580 µm variants for eLQFP but does not specify which applies to the eTQFP scenario, preventing exact geometry reconstruction.
Material thermal conductivity and volumetric heat capacity values (die, attach, epad, mold, board, leads) not tabulated; only weighted-average aggregates and qualitative descriptions provided.
Mesh discretization parameters (nx, ny, nz grid points, timestep nt) not disclosed; convergence criterion stated as ≤0.1% but reference geometry and validation mesh details absent.

TRIC source code, executable, mesh files, and supplementary material repository not linked or publicly accessible; validation against FloTHERM v12.2 relies on internal comparisons with no external reproduction pathway.
Boundary conditions cited to JEDEC JESD51-12 but full specification (convective heat transfer coefficients, radiation, symmetry planes, board extent) not reproduced in paper.
FloTHERM v12.2 setup parameters (mesh style, iterative solver tolerances, convergence criteria) not detailed; ~3% discrepancy attributed to mesh differences without quantitative reconciliation.

Figure 6 uses artificial instantaneous 1 W power step at t=0, not representative of realistic semiconductor workloads; no dynamic power profile, clock frequency, or die-level thermal coupling documented.

Package geometry simplified to Manhattan rectangular parallelepipeds with adiabatic symmetry planes; pLQFP die position shifts and multi-source layouts require ad-hoc projection basis adaptation not detailed for eTQFP.

TRIC is a model extraction and parameterization tool, not a direct 3D thermal solver; Figure 6 impedance curves are outputs of model-order reduction (MOR) applied to reduced-order parametric detailed thermal models (pDTMs), not raw FV solutions.

Steady-state junction-to-ambient thermal resistance ϑJA derived from compact thermal network; does not isolate individual thermal path contributions (lead, epad, mold) or enable localized thermal gradient analysis.
No uncertainty quantification for digitized impedance values from Figure 6 plot; estimated ±0.5 K/W margin assumes linear plot resolution but systematic reading error unvalidated.
Physical mismatch: simplified Manhattan geometry with weighted-average material properties vs. actual lead profiles, die attach thickness variation, and epad solder mask details.
Physical mismatch: idealized JEDEC boundary conditions (step function heat transfer coefficient) vs. realistic thermal interface material (TIM) behavior and board thermal resistance distribution.
